items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the social services law, in relation to enforcement of child day care safety and standards; to amend the penal law, in relation to making technical corrections thereto; and to repeal paragraph (b) of subdivision 12 of section 390 of the social services law relating to the use of single family dwellings for family day care or group family day care
items.lawCode: Amd §§390, 390-a & 410-x, rpld §390 sub 12 ¶(b), Soc Serv L; ren §260.30 to be §260.31, Pen L
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:A8827

TITLE OF BILL:  An act to amend the social services law, in relation to
enforcement of child day care safety and standards; to amend the penal
law, in relation to making technical corrections thereto; and to repeal
paragraph (b) of subdivision 12 of section 390 of the social services
law relating to the use of single family dwellings for family day care
or group family day care

Purpose of the bill:  This bill would enhance the availability of safe,
affordable, and accessible child day care; increase the child day care
capacity in group family day care homes; and improve quality enforcement
for all levels of child day care.

Summary of provisions:  Section 1 of the bill would amend Social
Services Law (SSL) §390(1)(d) and (e) to amend the definition of "group
family day care home" to increase the maximum number of children for
whom care may be provided under certain circumstances and to clarify
when an assistant must be present so the provisions parallel the
provisions for family day care homes. Section 1 would also amend the
definition of "family day care home" to provide that there must be one
caregiver for every two children under age two, consistent with the
requirements of a group family day care home.

Sections 2 and 3 of the bill would amend SSL §§390(2)(a) and
390(2)(d)(ii)(A), respectively, to provide that the Office of Children
and Family Services (OCFS) may issue an initial child day care license
or registration that is valid for a period of up to two years and subse-
quent licenses valid for a period of up to four years as long as the
provider remains substantially in compliance with applicable statutes
and regulations.

Section 4 of the bill would amend SSL §390(3)(b) to delete a provision
permitting a child day care provider to avoid a sanction by correcting
certain regulatory violations within thirty days of notification by
OCFS. The bill enables OCFS, in appropriate instances, to seek fines
and/or revocation of the provider's license or registration without
having to wait thirty days.

Section 5 of the bill would amend SSL §390(11)(c) to provide additional
exceptions to instances in which a child day care provider may rectify a
regulatory violation in order to avoid a sanction. The bill authorizes
OCFS to impose a sanction for the initial violation in these serious
situations even though the violation subsequently was corrected. The
bill would provide for a sanction where a provider or staff has injured
a child in care, failed to obtain necessary medical attention for a
child, used corporal punishment against a child, failed to report
suspected child abuse or maltreatment when required to do so, or submit-
ted a forged document to OCFS.

Section 6 of the bill would add a new paragraph (e) to SSL §390(11)
prohibiting the issuance of a license or registration to a child day

care provider whose license or registration was revoked or terminated
during the previous two years, unless OCFS determines that licensure or
registration would not jeopardize in any way the health, safety, or
welfare of the children for whom care would be provided. The prohibition
also applies to a child day care provider facing enforcement action who
surrenders a license or registration in order to avoid a suspension,
revocation, or termination. The prohibition will also apply to a child
day care program that is fined on two separate occasions for operating
without a required license or registration.

Section 7 of the bill would amend paragraph (a) of SSL §390(12), which
limits the ability of local governments to prohibit regulated family day
care or group family day care programs from operating in one, two or
multiple family dwellings, to also preclude restrictions and prohibi-
tions on such use. Section 8 would repeal paragraph (b) of SSL §390(12),
which is otherwise duplicative of paragraph (a) as amended.

Section 9 of the bill would amend SSL §390-a(3)(b)(ix) to limit mandated
staff training on the shaken baby syndrome to those day care programs
that legally may care for infants. The bill would exempt registered
school-age child care programs froth the training requirements, as those
programs cannot care for infants legally.

Section 10 of the bill would add a new subdivision seven to SSL §410-x
permitting a social services district to suspend an informal legally-ex-
empt provider from providing child care services funded under the New
York State Child Care Block Grant where the informal legally-exempt
provider is under investigation by child protective services as the
subject of a report of child abuse or maltreatment.

Section 11 of the bill renumbers Penal Law (PL) §260.30, as added by
Chapter 600 of the Laws of 1998, to §260.31 for the purpose of clarity,
as two PL sections numbered 260.30 were enacted in 1998.

Section 12 of the bill would provide for an immediate effective date.

Existing law:  SSL §390 defines child day care and governs the licensing
and registration of child day care providers by OCFS. It includes
authority for suspension or revocation of a license or registration and
civil penalties against child day care providers who violate applicable
statutes or regulations. The holder of a license or registration is
entitled to a hearing before OCFS prior to the imposition of any sanc-
tion. A child day care provider may avoid imposition of a penalty for
most regulatory and statutory violations by correcting the violation.
Even where the penalty imposed is the loss of the provider's license or
registration, the provider may apply to OCFS for a new license or regis-
tration almost immediately.

SSL §390-a sets forth standards and training requirements for child day
care providers. In 2004, legislation was enacted requiring training on
the shaken baby syndrome for all operators, program directors, employees

and assistants of child day care programs, including school-age child
care programs that cannot care for infants.

SSL §410-x governs the use of child day care subsidies by social
services districts and requires providers of legally-exempt child care
who receive subsidy funds to meet minimum health and safety standards.
Informal legally-exempt child care providers are not required to be
licensed or registered by OCFS. Informal legally-exempt child care
providers must be enrolled with a social services district to be eligi-
ble to provide subsidized child care.

Chapter 381 of the Laws of 1998 enacted PL § 260.30 pertaining to the
endangerment of vulnerable elderly adults.

Chapter 600 of the Laws of 1998 also enacted a PL § 260.30, known as
Jeremy and Julia's Law, which criminalized an intentional misrepresen-
tation by a child day care provider pertaining to: the number of chil-
dren in care; the area of the home, facility or center used for child
day care; or the credentials of the provider and/or staff where the
misrepresentation substantially places the health or safety of a child
at risk. Such a misrepresentation, when made to a parent, OCFS or law
enforcement agency, is a class A misdemeanor.

Chapter 416 of the Laws of 2000 enacted the Quality Child Care and
Protection Fund as State Finance Law § 97-www. Penalties assessed
against child day care providers are deposited in the fund. Monies in
the fund may be used for grants to child clay care providers for health
and safety purposes, for training of child day care providers' staff,
and for other activities to increase the availability and/or quality of
child day care programs.

Prior legislative history:  Portions of the bill were previously intro-
duced in 2004 as 5.6642. A substantially similar bill was introduced in
2008 as S.4545-A/A.10662-A and was referred to the Assembly Social
Services, Children and Families Committee and the Senate Rules Commit-
tee.

Statement in support:  The availability of safe, affordable, accessible
child care is important to working families and to families that other-
wise need child care for a portion of the day or week. Quality child
care enormously benefits the development of children and should be
available to families seeking such care. This proposal was generated in
response to these concerns and also results from discussions arising
from Governor Spitzer's Executive Order 12, which directed OCFS to meet
with representatives of child day care providers and discuss improve-
ments to the child day care system.

This proposal would expand the capacity of group family day care homes
by permitting the program to care for up to 12 children instead of the
current maximum of 10. A group family day care home could care for an
additional four school-age children during non-school periods instead of
the two additional children permitted under present law.  The proposal

would increase from seven to nine the number of children who could be
cared for by the operator of a group family day care home without an
assistant present. The proposal would also make consistent the require-
ment that a group family clay care home or a family day care home must
provide one caregiver for every two children under the age of two.

This proposal would enhance OCFS' ability to require child day care
providers to meet critical health and safety standards by further limit-
ing those instances where a provider who is in violation of a statutory
or regulatory requirement can avoid a penalty by merely fixing the
violation. In addition, a provider who has been penalized by the revoca-
tion or termination of a license or registration would be ineligible to
receive a new child day care license or registration for a period of two
years unless OCFS determines that the health, safety, or welfare of
children in care would not be jeopardized in any way. A provider who has
been sanctioned for illegal operation within the previous two years
would also be ineligible for a license or registration for two years.
These provisions would deter child day care providers from operating
substandard or illegal programs by increasing the potential consequences
for statutory and regulatory violations, while reducing the administra-
tive burden for those day care programs that are operating in compliance
with statute and regulations by extending the maximum term of renewal of
licenses and registrations to four years instead of two years.

This proposal would repeal a provision that generally precludes local
governments from prohibiting the use of one or two family dwellings or
multiple dwellings for family or group family day care if OCFS deter-
mines that the program meets the state's regulatory provisions, which
include health and fire safety requirements, for such programs.  SSL
§390(12)(a) includes a similar, more clearly worded restriction.  Howev-
er, the repealed paragraph goes beyond paragraph (a) to enable locali-
ties to preclude the Operation of certain family or group family day
care programs that have been approved by OCFS. This proposal would also
amend §390(12)(a)-to include in that paragraph the prohibition on
restricting use that is currently provided for in paragraph (b).

This proposal also provides a local social services district with the
authority to suspend the enrollment of an informal legally-exempt
provider who is being investigated for child abuse or maltreatment.  As
such, it provides much needed assistance to social services districts
that currently lack an effective means to safeguard a child receiving
subsidized child care from an informal legally-exempt provider who is
the subject of a report of abuse or maltreatment.

Budget implications:  This proposal is not expected to have a signif-
icant financial impact, although the funds deposited in the Quality
Child Care and Protection Fund may increase due to provisions expanding
the circumstances where OCFS may impose a penalty for statutory and
regulatory violations regardless of whether the violations have been
rectified.

Effective date:  This bill would take effect immediately.
